title: Business & email writing
theme: Professional written English — formal emails, job applications, cover letters, follow-ups, workplace messaging
goal: Student writes professional emails, applications, follow-ups and workplace messages with appropriate register, hedging, and clarity.
connects_to: A12 (academic writing) covers academic prose; A23 is workplace-specific. Pairs with A08 (hedging), A05 (passive), A10 (discourse markers).
module_chunks: Subject lines: "Following up on...", "Re: [topic]", "Quick question about..."
Formal openings: "I hope this email finds you well", "I'm reaching out regarding..."
Semi-formal openings: "Hope you're doing well", "Quick note about..."
Body chunks: "I'd like to...", "I'd appreciate it if...", "Would it be possible to..."
Cover letter chunks: "I am writing to apply for...", "I bring [X years] of experience in..."
Follow-up chunks: "Just following up on...", "Wanted to check in on...", "Any update on...?"
Hedging: "It might be worth considering...", "Perhaps we could...", "I'd suggest..."
Bad news softening: "Unfortunately...", "I regret to inform you..."
Apologizing: "Apologies for the delay...", "I appreciate your patience"

units.title: Email openings & closings
units.grammar_focus: Email openings and closings — matching register to relationship and purpose (formal, semi-formal, casual professional)
units.real_life_context: You open and close emails appropriately — neither too stiff for a coworker nor too casual for a client.

options: I hope this email finds you well.
grammar.answer: I hope this email finds you well.
grammar.explanation: "I hope this email finds you well" — quintessential formal email opener for first contact with senior or unknown recipients. Slightly clichéd but universally accepted. "Hi there!" and "Hey, what's up?" are too casual for formal contexts.

grammar.answer: Kind regards
grammar.explanation: "Kind regards" — formal closing for cover letters, applications, and emails to people you don't know well. "Best regards" is also fine. "Best" alone is semi-formal. "Cheers" is informal British. "Talk soon" is casual.

grammar.answer: Hope (or "Hoping")
grammar.explanation: "Hope you're doing well" — common semi-formal opener for someone you know but aren't close to. Drops the formal "I" of "I hope" to feel warmer. Widely used in workplace email.

grammar.hint: Too casual for a cold business email
grammar.answer: Dear [Name], I hope this email finds you well. I'm reaching out regarding...
grammar.explanation: "Hey there, what's going on?" is appropriate among friends but jarring in business cold-outreach. Cold emails need formal openings: "Dear [Name]" + "I hope this email finds you well" or "I'm reaching out regarding...". Register match is essential.

grammar.passage: Dear Ms. Silva, I hope this email finds you well. I'm reaching out regarding the position you advertised last week. Please find my CV attached for your consideration. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience aligns with your team's needs. Kind regards, Maria.
grammar.question: Identify the formal opener and the formal closer used.
grammar.answer: opener: "I hope this email finds you well"; closer: "Kind regards"
grammar.explanation: The email uses two formal anchors: "Dear Ms. Silva" + "I hope this email finds you well" at the opening; "Kind regards" at the closing. Both signal high register suitable for job applications.

listening_speaking.text: I hope this email finds you well.
Hope you're doing well.
I'm reaching out regarding...
Best regards / Kind regards.
Thanks again, talk soon.

roleplay.scenario: Charlotte plays a writing coach. You compose three email openings — formal, semi-formal, casual — for the same message but different recipients.
roleplay.opening_line: Imagine you need to ask three different people the same favour. Compose the opening line for each — formal, semi-formal, casual.

objectives.hint_en: Dear Ms. Costa, I hope this email finds you well. I'm reaching out to ask whether...

objectives.hint_en: Hi Marta, Hope you're doing well. Just wanted to ask if...

units.title: Job applications
units.grammar_focus: Job application email body — opening line, why-me paragraph, role fit, closing line
units.real_life_context: You write an application email that gets read, demonstrates fit, and ends with a clear ask for the next step.

options: I am writing to apply for the position of [role].
I would like to be hired.
grammar.answer: I am writing to apply for the position of [role].
grammar.explanation: "I am writing to apply for the position of [role] advertised on [source]" is the standard professional formula. Direct, clear, and signals competence. The other options are either too casual or grammatically awkward.

options: I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my background aligns with your team's needs.
grammar.answer: I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my background aligns with your team's needs.
grammar.explanation: This closing demonstrates: professional register ("I would welcome"), specific value framing ("how my background aligns"), and a soft ask for next step. The others lack specificity or sound desperate ("I really want this job").

grammar.answer: [number] (e.g., "five" or "ten")
grammar.explanation: "I bring [X] years of experience in [field], with a track record of [specific results]" — formula for quantifying experience with credibility. Always replace [X] with the actual number; "many" or "lots of" weakens the claim.

grammar.hint: Too casual for a formal application
grammar.answer: I am writing to apply for the Marketing position advertised on [LinkedIn / your website].
grammar.explanation: "Hello, I want to" is conversational; applications need formal phrasing: "I am writing to apply for [Position Name] advertised on [source]". Capitalize the position name; specify the source for tracking.

grammar.passage: Dear Hiring Manager, I am writing to apply for the Senior Designer position advertised on LinkedIn. I bring eight years of experience in product design, with a track record of leading design systems at scale. In my current role at [Company], I have shipped three major product launches that drove a 30% increase in user engagement. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my background aligns with your team's needs. Kind regards, Maria.
grammar.question: What three application elements are present in this paragraph?
grammar.answer: (1) formal opening with position name + source; (2) quantified experience + track record; (3) specific results + closing ask
grammar.explanation: A complete application body has three pillars: clear opening (formal + specific position + source), credibility (years + track record + specific results), and closing (welcome opportunity + soft ask). This template scales across roles and industries.

listening_speaking.text: I am writing to apply for the position of [role].
I bring [X] years of experience in [field].
In my current role, I have [specific achievement].
My background aligns with your team's needs.
I would welcome the opportunity to discuss.

units.title: Cover letters & CVs language
units.grammar_focus: Cover letter language and CV bullet points — strong action verbs, quantification, achievement framing
units.real_life_context: You craft cover letter paragraphs and CV bullets that highlight achievements with concrete impact.

options: Led cross-functional team of 12 to deliver a $2M product launch ahead of schedule.
grammar.answer: Led cross-functional team of 12 to deliver a $2M product launch ahead of schedule.
grammar.explanation: Strong CV bullet = action verb (Led) + scope (12 people) + outcome ($2M product launch) + qualifier (ahead of schedule). The others are vague and don't communicate value. Quantify everything possible.

grammar.answer: Spearheaded
grammar.explanation: "Spearheaded" = strong action verb showing initiative and ownership. Other options sound passive or weak. CV verbs to favour: Led, Spearheaded, Drove, Built, Launched, Scaled, Optimised, Restructured, Negotiated.

grammar.hint: Specific reason connecting your interests to the company
grammar.answer: [specific reason — e.g., "your commitment to sustainable design"]
grammar.explanation: "What draws me to [Company] is..." is a strong cover letter pivot showing you've researched the company. Always follow with a specific company value or initiative — generic "your innovative culture" reads as filler.

grammar.hint: Use a strong action verb + quantification
grammar.answer: Managed a team of [X] to deliver [specific outcome] resulting in [quantified impact].
grammar.explanation: Strong CV bullets follow the formula: [Strong action verb] + [scope/team] + [concrete deliverable] + [quantified impact]. "Did some stuff" is the antithesis of professional CV writing.

grammar.passage: What draws me to ClimateLab is your commitment to ocean restoration at scale — I've followed your work since the 2022 reef project. In my five years at Aquatic Research, I led the design of three monitoring platforms that are now deployed across 12 coastal sites. The technical challenge of building for hostile environments — combined with the urgency of the mission — is exactly the work I want to do for the next decade.
grammar.question: What three elements make this cover letter paragraph strong?
grammar.answer: (1) specific company research ("ocean restoration", "2022 reef project"); (2) quantified track record ("three monitoring platforms", "12 coastal sites"); (3) personal motivation tied to mission
grammar.explanation: Strong cover letter paragraphs do three things: show specific research (you know what they do), establish credibility (concrete achievements with numbers), and connect personal motivation to their mission. Each sentence does work.

listening_speaking.text: Led a cross-functional team of [X].
Spearheaded the initiative to [outcome].
What draws me to [Company] is...
My approach combines [skill A] with [skill B].
I'd contribute to [specific company goal].

units.title: Follow-ups & check-ins
units.grammar_focus: Follow-up emails after silence, post-meeting follow-ups, application follow-ups — gentle persistence without pushiness
units.real_life_context: You re-engage someone who hasn't responded — politely persistent without being annoying.

options: Just following up on my email below — wondering if you've had a chance to review.
grammar.answer: Just following up on my email below — wondering if you've had a chance to review.
grammar.explanation: "Just following up..." is the gold standard — polite, persistent, gives them an easy out ("had a chance to review"). The accusatory or anxious options damage relationships.

options: Following up on our conversation — happy to share more detail on [topic] if useful.
Hey, did we agree on something?
Just wanted to make sure you remember me.
grammar.answer: Following up on our conversation — happy to share more detail on [topic] if useful.
grammar.explanation: Post-meeting follow-up: reference the conversation, offer value ("happy to share more detail"), make it easy to engage. The other options sound either uncertain or pestering.

grammar.answer: Just checking in
grammar.explanation: "Just checking in on the [Position] application I submitted on [date]" — formal but warm follow-up for job applications. "Just checking in" is the universal gentle nudge phrase.

grammar.hint: Too aggressive — soften with "just following up"
grammar.answer: Hi [Name], just following up on my email from last week — wondering if you've had a chance to review.
grammar.explanation: "Did you read my email or what?" reads as hostile. Always soften with "just following up", "just checking in", or "wondering if you had a chance to review". The phrase "if you had a chance" acknowledges their time.

grammar.passage: Hi Maria, Just following up on my email from last Tuesday — wondering if you've had a chance to review the proposal. Happy to jump on a quick call this week if any questions came up. No rush on my end. Best, Pedro.
grammar.question: What three elements make this follow-up effective?
grammar.answer: (1) gentle opener "just following up"; (2) offer of value/easy engagement "happy to jump on a call"; (3) low-pressure close "no rush on my end"
grammar.explanation: Effective follow-ups combine gentle persistence ("just following up"), genuine helpfulness ("happy to jump on a call"), and pressure release ("no rush"). The recipient feels respected, not pressured.

listening_speaking.text: Just following up on my email.
Wondering if you had a chance to review.
Just checking in on [topic/application].
Happy to jump on a quick call.
No rush on my end.

units.title: Difficult emails
units.grammar_focus: Declining politely, delivering bad news, asking for raises/promotions, apologizing professionally
units.real_life_context: You handle the hardest emails — saying no, sharing bad news, advocating for yourself — with professional grace.

options: Thank you for thinking of me. Unfortunately, this isn't a fit for my current focus, but I'd be happy to recommend others.
grammar.answer: Thank you for thinking of me. Unfortunately, this isn't a fit for my current focus, but I'd be happy to recommend others.
grammar.explanation: Professional declines combine gratitude ("thank you"), reason ("isn't a fit for my current focus"), and offer of value ("happy to recommend others"). The others damage relationships or sound abrupt.

options: I'd like to discuss compensation given my expanded role and impact over the past 18 months.
grammar.answer: I'd like to discuss compensation given my expanded role and impact over the past 18 months.
grammar.explanation: Compensation conversations need: clear framing ("discuss compensation"), specific reasoning ("expanded role"), time anchor ("past 18 months"). "I want more money" or "I deserve" reads as demanding without justification.

grammar.answer: Unfortunately
grammar.explanation: "Unfortunately" — the standard bad news softener. Universal across formal contexts. Variants: "I regret to inform you that...", "Sadly...". Always pair with reason or path forward when possible.

grammar.hint: Too curt — soften with apology + alternative
grammar.answer: Unfortunately, I won't be able to attend the meeting on Friday — I have a competing commitment. Happy to follow up on the action items afterward.
grammar.explanation: Professional declines soften the no ("Unfortunately"), give a brief reason ("competing commitment"), and offer engagement ("happy to follow up"). "I'm busy" sounds dismissive.

grammar.passage: Hi João, Thanks for sending the proposal — I appreciate the work that went into it. Unfortunately, the budget for this project isn't going to allow us to move forward at the scope you've outlined. I'd love to keep the door open for a scaled-down version, or a future collaboration when budgets reset in Q1. Apologies for any inconvenience, and thanks again for putting it together. Best, Maria.
grammar.question: What three professional moves does this 'no' make?
grammar.answer: (1) gratitude/acknowledgment ("thanks for sending", "appreciate the work"); (2) clear reason ("budget isn't going to allow"); (3) keeps door open ("scaled-down version, or a future collaboration")
grammar.explanation: Strong declines preserve relationships. Three moves: acknowledge the effort, give a real reason, leave a door open. Never just say no — always frame the no with grace and a path forward.

listening_speaking.text: Unfortunately, this isn't a fit at this time.
I'd love to keep the door open for the future.
I regret to inform you that...
I'd like to discuss compensation given...
Apologies for any inconvenience this may cause.

objectives.hint_en: Open with appreciation: 'Thank you for thinking of us for this — the relationship means a lot.' Then soften the no: 'Unfortunately, the timing doesn't work on our end right now.'

objectives.hidden_prompt: user suggests adding a brief honest reason
objectives.hint_en: Give a real but brief reason — 'we're at capacity through Q3' or 'we're shifting focus on internal work this year'. Honesty preserves trust.

objectives.hidden_prompt: user advises closing with future option
objectives.hint_en: Close with: 'I'd love to keep the conversation open for Q4 or beyond — when the timing aligns, we'd jump at the chance to work with you again.'

guided_chat.suggested_script:
**Script** (referencial, 7 turnos):

1. **Charlotte**: "I need to tell a longtime client we can't take their new project. Two years of work, but the timing isn't right. I don't want to ruin the relationship."
2. **Student**: "Open with appreciation: 'Thank you for thinking of us for this — the relationship means a lot.' Then soften the no: 'Unfortunately, the timing doesn't work on our end right now.'"
3. **Charlotte**: "Good. How honest should I be about why?"
4. **Student**: "Give a real but brief reason — 'we're at capacity through Q3' or 'we're shifting focus on internal work this year'. Honesty preserves trust."
5. **Charlotte**: "And how do I leave it open without overpromising?"
6. **Student**: "Close with: 'I'd love to keep the conversation open for Q4 or beyond — when the timing aligns, we'd jump at the chance to work with you again.'"
7. **Charlotte**: "OK, drafting it now. Thanks for the structure."

> A05 chat = full LLM. Scaffold via hint_pt/hint_en.

cross_unit_consolidation: Choose email register (formal / semi-formal / casual professional) appropriate to recipient
Write professional job application emails with formal opener + quantified experience + closing ask
Craft strong CV bullets with action verb + scope + quantified outcome
Send polite follow-ups using "just following up", "just checking in", "wondering if you had a chance"
Handle difficult emails: declines (gratitude + reason + door open), bad news (softener + reason + path forward), raise requests (framing + impact + clear ask)
Always close professional emails with appropriate sign-off ("Kind regards" / "Best regards" / "Best")
Soften bad news with "Unfortunately" and apologize professionally with "Apologies for any inconvenience"
Preserve relationships even when saying no
